It really depends on the employee and their circumstances. Just to be clear though, I think that apprenticeships are good for proper professions (e.g. eletricians, nurses and so on), but I draw the line when it comes to jobs that can be learnt within a day or two.

But the cop is tailing me, and I feel like he's just waiting for me to screw up, or he's in a hurry, so I move over to the right lane, but I didn't signal...that's when the lights flipped on. My first thought was "oh fuck, here we go." I didn't have any gum, or water to sip on to hide any smell of alcohol on my breath. He taps on my window and asks if I had been drinking, I tell him no, then he says, "Really?" At that point, I knew it was kinda obvious I might have had a couple. So I tell him I had a couple an hour or two ago. He does the follow-the-light test, and my eyes lag. I walk in a straight line okay, but the stand-on-one foot test was conducted on a bridge in the dead of winter with it beginning to sleet and I was wearing a t-shirt (no chance to put on my jacket). Then he arrests me on suspicion of DUI, and then asks if anyone can get my car, and I say that my brother can, so my brother and my parents come to get my car... saved me an impound fee. That sucked.

I get to the jail, and I blow a 0.07 BAC; DUI is 0.08, but anything above 0.05 and below 0.08 is DWI, which is enough to get you arrested where I'm from. It could have been a lot worse, but ultimately my bail was $1200. My parents bailed me out that morning, but it was pretty fucking awful. Had to pay to go to DUI school, pay a fee in lieu of doing community service, as well as the cost of the charges, AND because it is unsupervised probation, I have monthly fees to pay to the DA until August of NEXT YEAR.

I thought I was good to drive. And had I been in the state where I currently reside, rather than where my parents live, I would have been FINE. No charges. Nothing. I wasn't swerving. No one was on the road at the time except for me and the cop. I wasn't endangering anyone. It is such bullshit. Getting arrested made me realize that literally EVERYTHING is a fucking money game to the court and the state. Lawyer was $750, Bail Bondsman was $200, cost of charges levied by the court were around $1200, the cost in lieu of community service was $150, DUI school cost $300, and then it's something like $40 each month for 18 months ($720) to the DA. All in all, it was around $4040. Fucking hell.

On the bright side, if I don't fuck up again where the charges were at (I'm rarely there to begin with), I'll have it off my record in 12 months.
Pay money to the DA's office. I dunno. Like I said, the whole thing is a money grab.

Dear Kimmybjonsson,

 

Seeds are vital for life and essential for food production. Whoever controls seeds, controls our food. In May I went to Ghana to talk to small-scale farmers fighting the controversial Plant Breeders Bill that would promote the use of corporate seeds.

If the bill is passed, power over seeds and food production will be taken away from Ghanaian small-scale farmers, and handed to big business. Generations of agricultural knowledge, culture and tradition will be lost. Shockingly, our government is backing an aid scheme which is supporting the bill.

http://i.imgur.com/YEFvbrD.jpg

Small-scale farmers produce 70% of Africa's food, and women are often the main producers. The Ghanaian women I met save and swap seeds each year. As Esther, a farmer in central Ghana, explained to me, My mother gave me some seeds to plant. And I'm also giving those seeds to my children to plant. And that is how all the women are doing it.

 

Through the G7 initiative known as the New Alliance for Food Security and Nutrition, the UK government is pushing a pro-corporate seed agenda on countries such as Ghana with 600 million from the aid budget. But corporate seeds do not benefit small-scale famers and threaten to replace indigenous seeds. Farmers say corporate seeds only work for one season and require expensive and harmful chemicals to produce a decent yield. They could even be imprisoned for saving corporate seeds, meaning they must be bought each year.

 

Under the New Alliance, small-scale farmers stand to lose. As Patricia Dianon, president of the Rural Womens Farmers Association of Ghana, told me, "If we throw away our traditional seeds and we take the corporate seeds, where will we get seed to sow? Are we not in slavery?"

The good news is resistance in Ghana is working. Click here to donate and find out how you'll be helping us campaign alongside Ghanaian activists.

By taking to the streets in Ghana, activists have succeeded in stalling the legislation. Here in the UK, we need to up the pressure on our government and stop it supporting corporate seeds and handing power over food systems in Africa to big business.

 

With your help we can promote alternative farming techniques that put people first.

Best wishes,

Heidi Chow,

Campaigner, Global Justice Now
